simple: the part of the operating system that runs with full control of the machine.
analogy: the principal.
precise: the privileged program that manages the CPU, memory and devices and offers services to other programs. Not the same as a "kernel (GPU)" in F6, which is a function launched on a GPU.
source: D1 of F3-18 (Intel Corporation, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: C++ without the operating system's help: only a small part of the standard library is guaranteed.
analogy: the principal on the first morning, with no secretary.
precise: an implementation in which a program may run without an operating system; only a limited set of headers is required, and program start-up and termination are implementation-defined.
source: D8 of F3-18 (ISO/IEC 14882 (C++), working draft for C++20) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a kernel whose addresses are at the very top of the virtual address space.
analogy: the staff rooms are on the top floor, far from the classrooms.
precise: a kernel linked at virtual addresses in the upper half of the canonical address space (here 0xffffffff80000000 + physical address), so that the lower half stays free for user programs.
source: D1 of F3-18 (Intel Corporation, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3); R1 of F3-18 (lab run university/labs/F3-18/elfcheck.log) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the CPU's 64-bit mode.
analogy: the school's full-day timetable, as opposed to the morning set-up hour.
precise: the x86-64 operating mode entered with paging enabled, PAE set and the long-mode-enable bit set in the EFER register; 64-bit code runs in its 64-bit sub-mode.
source: D1 of F3-18 (Intel Corporation, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part of a program for variables that start at zero; the file does not store those zeros.
analogy: wiping the blackboard before the day starts.
precise: a section of type NOBITS that occupies memory but no file space; the loader or start-up code must fill it with zeros.
source: D9 of F3-18 ("System V Application Binary Interface" generic ABI, ELF chapters) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: code that sets up a global object before main (here kmain) runs.
analogy: the assistants who set up their tables before the first lesson.
precise: dynamic initialisation of objects with static storage duration; on ELF x86-64 the compiler places a pointer to each translation unit's initialisation function in .init_array, which start-up code must call.
source: D3 of F3-18 ("Itanium C++ ABI"); R5 of F3-18 (forensic runs forensic_diff.log, forensic_boot.log, forensic_elf.log) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an agreement between a loader and a kernel about how the kernel is found, loaded and started.
analogy: the sheet of paper the key holder hands to the principal.
precise: a boot protocol: the kernel image carries a header with a magic number and flags; the loader enters the kernel in 32-bit protected mode with a magic value in EAX and the address of an information structure in EBX.
source: D2 of F3-18 (Free Software Foundation, "Multiboot Specification" version 1) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the simplest way for a computer to send text, one bit after another over a wire.
analogy: the hand-held radio to the caretaker.
precise: a universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter; the PC's first one (COM1) is a 16550-compatible device at I/O port 0x3F8.
source: D4 of F3-18 (National Semiconductor (now Texas Instruments), "PC16550D Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter with FIFOs" datasheet) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the kernel's "I cannot continue" stop.
analogy: the principal closing the school and posting one clear notice on the door.
precise: a function that disables interrupts, prints the location and reason of a fatal error, and halts (here: ends QEMU with a failure status).
source: R3 of F3-18 (lab run assert.log) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a table that describes the code and data "segments" the CPU may use.
analogy: the list of room types in the school: staff rooms and student rooms.
precise: a table of segment descriptors (8 bytes each, system descriptors 16 bytes in 64-bit mode) located by GDTR; in 64-bit mode code descriptors still set the mode (L bit) and the privilege level (DPL), while bases and limits are mostly ignored.
source: D1 of F3-19 (Intel Corporation, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small structure that tells the CPU which stack to use when an interrupt arrives.
analogy: the noticeboard that says which staircase to take.
precise: in 64-bit mode, a 104-byte structure holding RSP0–RSP2 (stacks for privilege changes), IST1–IST7 (stacks selected by IDT gates) and the I/O permission bitmap base; loaded with ltr.
source: D1 of F3-19 (Intel Corporation, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the table of handlers, one per interrupt or exception number.
analogy: the list on the office wall: event number → who handles it.
precise: up to 256 16-byte gate descriptors located by IDTR; each holds a handler address, a code selector, a type (interrupt or trap gate), a DPL and an IST index.
source: D1 of F3-19 (Intel Corporation, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the CPU's own alarm when an instruction cannot be completed normally.
analogy: an accident in a classroom, reported by the room itself.
precise: a synchronous event generated by the processor (vectors 0–31), classified as a fault (restartable; the saved RIP points at the faulting instruction), a trap (the saved RIP points after it) or an abort.
source: D1 of F3-19 (Intel Corporation, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a signal that makes the CPU stop what it is doing and run a handler.
analogy: the doorbell.
precise: an asynchronous event from a device or another CPU, delivered through an interrupt controller with a vector number; handled through the same IDT as exceptions.
source: D1 of F3-19 (Intel Corporation, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: up to seven spare stacks the CPU can switch to for chosen interrupts.
analogy: the emergency staircase.
precise: seven 64-bit stack pointers in the TSS; a gate whose IST field is n (1–7) makes the CPU load RSP from ISTn unconditionally before pushing the frame.
source: D1 of F3-19 (Intel Corporation, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3); R2 of F3-19 (lab run exceptions.log) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the CPU's report that it failed while trying to report another fault.
analogy: the messenger trips on the stairs on the way to report the accident.
precise: exception 8, raised when a second exception occurs while delivering a first one in certain combinations (for example a page fault while delivering a page fault); an abort with error code 0.
source: D1 of F3-19 (Intel Corporation, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a failure while reporting a double fault; the CPU gives up and resets.
analogy: the school is evacuated and nobody writes a report.
precise: an exception during delivery of a double fault; the processor enters shutdown, which the platform turns into a reset.
source: D1 of F3-19 (Intel Corporation, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3); R4 of F3-19 (forensic runs forensic_serial.log and forensic_int.log) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the register that holds the address a page fault was about.
analogy: the room number on the accident report.
precise: control register 2, loaded by the processor with the linear address that caused a page fault.
source: D1 of F3-19 (Intel Corporation, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one 4 KiB piece of real memory.
analogy: one cupboard.
precise: a naturally aligned 4 KiB block of physical address space, the unit the page tables map (larger page sizes are multiples of it).
source: D1 of F3-20 (Intel Corporation, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the firmware's list of which address ranges are RAM you may use and which are not.
analogy: the caretaker's room plan.
precise: a list of (base, length, type) entries delivered by the firmware or loader (BIOS E820 through Multiboot here, the UEFI memory map in A3); only "available" ranges may be used freely.
source: D2 of F3-20 (Free Software Foundation, "Multiboot Specification" version 1); D3 of F3-20 (UEFI Forum, "Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) Specification") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part of the kernel that hands out and takes back frames.
analogy: the cupboard office.
precise: an allocator over physical frames, built from the memory map, offering allocation of single frames and of contiguous, aligned runs.
source: D4 of F3-20 (Remzi H. Arpaci-Dusseau and Andrea C. Arpaci-Dusseau, "Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one bit per frame: 1 used, 0 free.
analogy: a tick list with one box per cupboard.
precise: a frame allocator whose state is a bit array; allocation searches for a clear bit (or a run of them).
source: D4 of F3-20 (Remzi H. Arpaci-Dusseau and Andrea C. Arpaci-Dusseau, "Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an allocator that keeps memory in blocks of 1, 2, 4, 8… frames, splitting big blocks and joining neighbours back.
analogy: cupboards grouped in pairs, pairs of pairs, and so on; a returned cupboard rejoins its partner when the partner is free.
precise: a power-of-two allocator: a block of order k has 2^k frames and is aligned to 2^k frames; its buddy is found by flipping bit k of its frame number; freeing merges buddies recursively.
source: D5 of F3-20 (Donald E. Knuth, "The Art of Computer Programming", Volume 1, section on dynamic storage allocation (the buddy system)); D6 of F3-20 (Daniel P. Bovet and Marco Cesati, "Understanding the Linux Kernel") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the size class of a buddy block, as a power of two.
analogy: "a group of 2^order cupboards".
precise: the exponent k of a block of 2^k frames; this kernel uses orders 0 (4 KiB) to 10 (4 MiB).
source: R2 of F3-20 (lab runs mem_128M.log, mem_1G.log, mem_4G.log) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: enough free memory in total, but not enough of it in one piece.
analogy: many free cupboards, none of them next to another free one.
precise: the state in which free memory is split into blocks smaller than a request, so the request fails although the free total exceeds it.
source: D5 of F3-20 (Donald E. Knuth, "The Art of Computer Programming", Volume 1, section on dynamic storage allocation (the buddy system)); R4 of F3-20 (forensic run forensic_leak.log) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a window in the kernel's address space where every physical address can be read at a fixed offset.
analogy: a master key that opens every cupboard by its number.
precise: a virtual range (here 0xffff800000000000 + physical) mapping all of RAM, used by the kernel to touch frames it does not otherwise map.
source: R1 of F3-20 (lab run university/labs/F3-20/pmm_host.log) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the table the CPU uses to turn the addresses a program uses into real memory addresses.
analogy: the map of lockers: locker number to real cupboard.
precise: in x86-64 4-level paging, a hierarchy of 4 KiB tables of 512 eight-byte entries (PML4, PDPT, PD, PT) rooted at CR3; each entry holds a physical address and permission bits.
source: D1 of F3-21 (Intel Corporation, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the top-level page table.
analogy: the first binder of the locker map.
precise: the page-map level-4 table whose physical address is in CR3; indexed by virtual address bits 47–39.
source: D1 of F3-21 (Intel Corporation, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3); R3 of F3-21 (lab run walk.log) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one line of a page table: where the page is and what may be done with it.
analogy: one line of the locker map, with "staff only" and "look, don't touch" marks.
precise: a 64-bit entry: present, writable, user, write-through, cache-disable, accessed, dirty, page-size or PAT, global, the physical address bits, and NX in bit 63.
source: D1 of F3-21 (Intel Corporation, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3); R1 of F3-21 (lab run university/labs/F3-21/pte_host.log) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the CPU's small cache of recent translations.
analogy: the principal's sticky note of recently looked-up lockers.
precise: a processor cache of virtual-to-physical translations and their rights; not kept coherent with the page tables by hardware, so software must invalidate entries it changes (invlpg, a CR3 write, or other mechanisms).
source: D1 of F3-21 (Intel Corporation, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3); R4 of F3-21 (forensic runs forensic_tlb.log and forensic_fixed.log, exit code 33 each.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a mark that says "this page holds data; never run it as code".
analogy: a "no experiments in this room" sign.
precise: bit 63 of a paging entry, honoured when EFER.NXE is set; an instruction fetch from such a page raises a page fault with the instruction-fetch bit set.
source: D1 of F3-21 (Intel Corporation, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3); R2 of F3-21 (lab run b4.log) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an address deliberately left unmapped next to a stack or buffer, so running off the end faults.
analogy: the empty cupboard number at the end of the row that rings an alarm.
precise: an unmapped page adjacent to a region that grows; an access raises a page fault instead of corrupting the neighbouring memory.
source: R2 of F3-21 (lab run b4.log) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a translation the CPU keeps even when it switches to another program's tables.
analogy: the staff lockers that are on every class's page.
precise: a leaf entry with the G bit set, while CR4.PGE is enabled; such TLB entries survive CR3 writes and are removed with invlpg or by toggling CR4.PGE.
source: D1 of F3-21 (Intel Corporation, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a table that lets each page choose how the CPU caches it.
analogy: a choice of delivery methods per cupboard: keep a copy on the desk, or always walk to the cupboard.
precise: an MSR with eight memory-type entries; the PAT, PCD and PWT bits of a leaf entry select one, giving write-back, write-through, write-combining, uncached and other types per page.
source: D1 of F3-21 (Intel Corporation, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: all the addresses a program can use, whether or not memory is behind them.
analogy: all the locker numbers that could exist.
precise: with 4-level paging, 48-bit canonical addresses: a lower half 0–0x00007fffffffffff and an upper half 0xffff800000000000–0xffffffffffffffff.
source: D1 of F3-21 (Intel Corporation, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part of the kernel that hands out memory of any size, like new does in programs.
analogy: the stationery cupboard.
precise: a general-purpose allocator for kernel objects, built on the physical memory manager and the kernel page tables, offering kmalloc/kfree and the C++ allocation functions.
source: D1 of F3-22 (Jeff Bonwick, "The Slab Allocator: An Object-Caching Kernel Memory Allocator", USENIX Summer 1994 Technical Conference) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an allocator that cuts larger pieces of memory into many equal objects.
analogy: a drawer divided into equal compartments.
precise: an object-caching allocator in which each cache holds slabs (contiguous memory blocks) divided into objects of one size; Bonwick's design adds constructors and per-CPU layers that this chapter leaves out.
source: D1 of F3-22 (Jeff Bonwick, "The Slab Allocator: An Object-Caching Kernel Memory Allocator", USENIX Summer 1994 Technical Conference) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one fixed object size the heap serves, such as 64 bytes.
analogy: one labelled box.
precise: in this heap, one of eight caches for 16, 32, …, 2048 bytes, each a list of 16 KiB slabs; a request is served by the smallest class at least as large as the size and the alignment.
source: R2 of F3-22 (lab run b5.log) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: filling freed memory with a known pattern so that later writes to it can be detected.
analogy: bright tape on every returned item.
precise: writing a constant byte (here 0xDE) over a freed object and verifying the pattern when the object is handed out again; a mismatch reports a write after free.
source: R3 of F3-22 (lab run uaf.log) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: using memory after giving it back.
analogy: writing in an exercise book after returning it.
precise: an access through a pointer to an object whose storage has been released; undefined behaviour in C++, and a classic source of kernel memory corruption.
source: D2 of F3-22 (ISO/IEC 14882 (C++), working draft for C++20) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the versions of operator new and delete a program may define itself.
analogy: the school writing its own stationery rules.
precise: the global operator new, new[], delete and delete[] in their plain, sized, aligned (std::align_val_t) and nothrow forms, whose definitions a program may provide to replace the library's.
source: D2 of F3-22 (ISO/IEC 14882 (C++), working draft for C++20) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a linked list whose links are stored inside the objects themselves.
analogy: students holding hands in a line instead of being written on a list.
precise: a list in which each element contains its own link member, so insertion and removal need no allocation.
source: R2 of F3-22 (lab run b5.log) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: memory that was taken and never given back.
analogy: pencils that never come back to the cupboard.
precise: allocated storage no longer reachable or no longer intended to be used but never freed; measured here as the difference in free frames before and after a workload.
source: R2 of F3-22 (lab run b5.log) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a block of memory whose bytes are the pixels on the screen.
analogy: the noticeboard: what you pin there is what people see.
precise: a region of (usually device) memory in which each pixel has a fixed position and format; in this lab, 640 × 480 pixels of 32 bits (0x00RRGGBB), one row after another, mapped from the display device's BAR0.
source: D2 of F3-23 (UEFI Forum, "Unified Extensible Firmware Interface Specification") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: letters stored as little grids of on and off pixels.
analogy: stencils for the noticeboard.
precise: a table mapping each character to a fixed-size pixel pattern; this course draws its own 5 × 7 font in a 6 × 10 cell.
source: R2 of F3-23 (lab run screen.log) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a label saying how important a message is.
analogy: "for your information", "warning", "emergency" on a notice.
precise: an ordered severity (here Debug < Info < Warn < Error) attached to each message, used to filter output and to choose its colour.
source: R1 of F3-23 (lab run university/labs/F3-23/boot.log) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: tables in which the firmware describes the machine: maker, model, firmware version.
analogy: the plaque at the school gate.
precise: the DMTF System Management BIOS specification: an entry point (found by an anchor string, 32-bit "_SM_" or 64-bit "_SM3_") gives the address of a table of typed structures (type 0 firmware, type 1 system, type 2 baseboard, …), each a formatted area followed by strings.
source: D3 of F3-23 (DMTF, "System Management BIOS (SMBIOS) Reference Specification") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a way for the CPU to collect several writes and send them to a device together.
analogy: carrying a whole stack of notices to the board in one trip.
precise: a memory type in which writes may be buffered and merged before reaching memory, with weak ordering; selected for a page through the PAT (F3-21).
source: D4 of F3-23 (Intel, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: waiting for something that will never happen, because the one who could make it happen is waiting too (or is you).
analogy: the principal waiting for the microphone key the deputy will never return.
precise: a state in which a set of execution contexts each wait for a resource held by another member of the set; here a CPU spinning for a lock it already holds.
source: D5 of F3-23 (Remzi H. Arpaci-Dusseau and Andrea C. Arpaci-Dusseau, "Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the kernel's emergency state, in which it only tries to report and stop.
analogy: the fire alarm rule: nobody waits for the key.
precise: in this kernel, a flag set once by the panic or fatal-exception path; from then on output ignores the output lock and the framebuffer switches to the panic screen.
source: R3 of F3-23 (lab run panic_lock.log) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a picture of the emulated screen, saved by QEMU.
analogy: a photograph of the noticeboard.
precise: the QEMU monitor command screendump FILE, which writes the display's current contents as an image (PPM by default).
source: D6 of F3-23 (QEMU documentation) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: tables in memory in which the firmware describes the machine's devices and wiring.
analogy: the caretaker's booklet.
precise: the Advanced Configuration and Power Interface; here only its static tables: a Root System Description Pointer, a root table (RSDT with 32-bit or XSDT with 64-bit entries), and description tables each starting with a 36-byte header with signature, length and checksum.
source: D1 of F3-24 (UEFI Forum, "Advanced Configuration and Power Interface (ACPI) Specification") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the small signpost that tells you where the ACPI tables are.
analogy: the note on the office door saying "booklet in drawer 3".
precise: the Root System Description Pointer, a structure with the signature "RSD PTR " found on a 16-byte boundary in the first KiB of the EBDA or in 0xE0000–0xFFFFF on legacy boots (UEFI passes it in the configuration table).
source: D1 of F3-24 (UEFI Forum, "Advanced Configuration and Power Interface (ACPI) Specification") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the ACPI table that lists the interrupt hardware.
analogy: the booklet's page about doorbells and desks.
precise: the Multiple APIC Description Table (signature "APIC"): local APIC address, flags (PCAT_COMPAT), then variable-length entries for processor local APICs, I/O APICs, interrupt source overrides, NMI sources and their x2APIC variants.
source: D1 of F3-24 (UEFI Forum, "Advanced Configuration and Power Interface (ACPI) Specification") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: each CPU's own interrupt receiver.
analogy: the receiver on a staff desk.
precise: the per-processor Advanced Programmable Interrupt Controller: it accepts interrupts, prioritises them by vector (in-service, request and priority registers), delivers them to the core, and has its own timer and local vector table; accessed as memory (xAPIC) or MSRs (x2APIC).
source: D2 of F3-24 (Intel, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the chip that turns device interrupt wires into messages to CPUs.
analogy: the switchboard.
precise: an I/O APIC with a redirection table of one 64-bit entry per input pin (vector, delivery mode, polarity, trigger mode, mask, destination), programmed through an index register and a data window.
source: D3 of F3-24 (Intel, "82093AA I/O Advanced Programmable Interrupt Controller (IOAPIC)" datasheet) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the old interrupt controller of the original PC.
analogy: the old bell board with eight lamps.
precise: a pair of cascaded 8259A Programmable Interrupt Controllers providing ISA IRQs 0–15; still emulated, and by default delivering on vectors that collide with CPU exceptions, so it must be remapped and masked.
source: D4 of F3-24 (Intel, "8259A Programmable Interrupt Controller" datasheet) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: ACPI's number for an interrupt input, counted across all IOAPICs.
analogy: the switchboard's line number.
precise: a flat numbering of IOAPIC inputs; an IOAPIC with first GSI g serves g to g + pins − 1.
source: D1 of F3-24 (UEFI Forum, "Advanced Configuration and Power Interface (ACPI) Specification") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a note that an old IRQ number arrives on a different line, or with different electrical settings.
analogy: "the old bell 0 now arrives on line 2".
precise: a MADT entry mapping an ISA IRQ to a GSI, with flags for polarity (bits 1:0) and trigger mode (bits 3:2), where 0 means "conforms to the bus" (ISA: edge, active high).
source: D1 of F3-24 (UEFI Forum, "Advanced Configuration and Power Interface (ACPI) Specification") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: telling the interrupt controller "I have finished with that interrupt".
analogy: pressing "done" on the desk receiver.
precise: a write to the local APIC's EOI register that clears the highest-priority bit in the in-service register, allowing interrupts of equal or lower priority to be delivered again.
source: D2 of F3-24 (Intel, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the newer mode of the local APIC, used through special CPU registers instead of memory.
analogy: a desk receiver with a direct line instead of a shared cable.
precise: an extension of the local APIC architecture with 32-bit APIC IDs, register access through MSRs 0x800–0x8FF, and a single 64-bit ICR; enabled by bit 10 of IA32_APIC_BASE.
source: D2 of F3-24 (Intel, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the counter the kernel reads to know what time it is.
analogy: the hall clock or the desk counter.
precise: a monotonically increasing hardware counter with a known rate, read by now_ns(); here the TSC or the HPET main counter.
source: D5 of F3-25 (The Linux kernel documentation and source) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a clock that never goes backwards.
analogy: a clock nobody is allowed to set back.
precise: a time base whose successive reads are non-decreasing, unaffected by changes to wall-clock time; required for timeouts and intervals.
source: D5 of F3-25 (The Linux kernel documentation and source) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a precise timer chip with one fast counter and a few alarms.
analogy: the accurate hall clock.
precise: the High Precision Event Timer: a memory-mapped block with a main counter of fixed period (at most 100 ns), and several comparators; described by the ACPI "HPET" table.
source: D1 of F3-25 (Intel, "IA-PC HPET (High Precision Event Timers) Specification") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the old timer chip of the PC, with 16-bit counters.
analogy: the gym teacher's stopwatch that only counts to 65,535.
precise: the Intel 8254 Programmable Interval Timer: three 16-bit down-counters at 1,193,182 Hz; channel 0 drives IRQ 0, channel 2 is gated by port 0x61 and readable through its output bit.
source: D3 of F3-25 (Intel, "8254 Programmable Interval Timer" datasheet) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a counter inside the CPU that goes up very fast.
analogy: the desk counter.
precise: a 64-bit per-CPU counter read with rdtsc; its rate is not reported directly on many CPUs and must be measured.
source: D2 of F3-25 (Intel, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a TSC that ticks at the same rate whatever the CPU's speed or sleep state.
analogy: a desk counter that does not slow down when the principal does.
precise: a TSC that runs at a constant rate in all ACPI P-, C- and T-states, reported by CPUID leaf 0x80000007, EDX bit 8.
source: D2 of F3-25 (Intel, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the alarm built into each CPU's interrupt receiver.
analogy: the alarm clock on the principal's desk.
precise: the local APIC's timer: an initial-count register counting down at the bus or core crystal rate divided by a configurable divisor, raising the vector in its LVT entry in one-shot, periodic or TSC-deadline mode.
source: D2 of F3-25 (Intel, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual", Volume 3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a timer set only for the next thing that must happen, instead of ringing regularly.
analogy: setting the alarm for the next appointment only.
precise: programming a one-shot timer for the earliest pending deadline; no interrupts arrive while nothing is due.
source: D5 of F3-25 (The Linux kernel documentation and source) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the list of things waiting for a time, earliest first.
analogy: the principal's appointment book.
precise: a priority queue of timers keyed by deadline; the timer interrupt runs every expired timer, re-queues periodic ones and re-arms the hardware for the new head.
source: R1 of F3-25 (lab run university/labs/F3-25/clock_host.log) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
